title: Lighting for needlework
subtitle: How to set up task lighting that shows thread colour accurately and reduces eye strain.
excerpt: Poor lighting is responsible for more errors and more eyestrain in embroidery than almost any other factor. The position and colour temperature of the light affects whether the thread colours appear accurate and whether the stitch texture is visible. This reading covers what to look for and where to place it.
sourceNotes: Lighting ergonomics guidance synthesised from contemporary needlework practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The warmth or coolness of a light source, measured in Kelvin. Warm bulbs (2700K) render colour differently from daylight bulbs (5500K to 6500K). Daylight-temperature bulbs are standard in needlework and colour-matching work because they show thread colours close to how they appear in natural light.

content.text: affects how thread and fabric colours appear under artificial light. Under warm domestic bulbs, blues read as darker and greens shift towards yellow. Under daylight bulbs, colours appear close to their natural state. Thread selection done under the wrong light produces jarring results in daylight.

Choose a task lamp with a daylight LED bulb rated 5000K to 6500K. Avoid warm-white bulbs (2700K to 3000K) for colour-critical embroidery. Natural daylight is the gold standard; work near a north-facing window in daylight hours when selecting thread colours.

Position the light to your non-dominant side, directed at an angle across the work surface. This angled light shows the texture of the stitches by casting micro-shadows across the threads. Light from directly above flattens texture and makes stitching harder to see.

Glare off the fabric surface causes squinting and eye fatigue. Matte cotton and linen reflect less glare than satin-finish fabrics. If the fabric is reflective, drape a piece of matte tissue paper over the area not being stitched to reduce the reflected light reaching your eyes.

Never select thread colours under warm domestic lighting if the piece will be displayed in natural light. Take skeins to the nearest window or use a daylight lamp for matching. A thread that matches perfectly under a warm 2700K bulb can clash noticeably in natural light.
